n: Gonococci inside neutrophils on Gram stain

ww.Staphylococcus aureus in pus: Staphylococcus aureus is gram-positive, so its cocci stain deep purple and pile into irregular grape-like clusters, often lying outside the cells. These organisms stain pink-red, come in pairs with flattened touching sides, and sit inside the neutrophil cytoplasm.
ww.Streptococcus pneumoniae diplococci: Pneumococci are gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci that stain purple and are often surrounded by a clear capsule halo. These pairs stain pink-red, are bean-shaped, and have no capsule halo around them, as expected for the unencapsulated gonococcus.
ww.Chlamydia trachomatis inclusions: Chlamydia is not seen on a Gram stain. Its glycogen-rich inclusions show in infected epithelial cells on Giemsa or iodine stains, as a single cytoplasmic mass, not as many separate pairs of cocci inside white cells.
ww.Haemophilus ducreyi in chains: Haemophilus ducreyi, the cause of chancroid, is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that lines up in chains, the school of fish pattern, in smears from a genital ulcer. Here the organisms are rounded pairs scattered inside neutrophils, not chains.

look: Look at the two large neutrophils, one at center left and one at upper center. Each has a lobed pink nucleus, and its cytoplasm is peppered with tiny pink-magenta pairs of round bacteria, so the organisms are gram-negative and intracellular. Each pair has flattened, touching sides like a coffee bean. Gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils in a genital specimen mean Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

findings: Neutrophil, center left: a polymorphonuclear cell with a pink lobed nucleus holds dozens of tiny paired cocci in its cytoplasm. Seeing the organisms inside the white cell is the pattern typical of gonococci in pus.

Neutrophil, upper center: a second white cell carries the same pink-magenta pairs, so intracellular organisms recur across the smear. The pink color means a thin peptidoglycan wall that lost the crystal violet at decolorization, so the bacteria are gram-negative.

Free pair: a few diplococci lie outside the cells, for example just below the center-left neutrophil. Most gonococci sit inside neutrophils in acute infection, but some are found free in the background.

Surrounding neutrophils: the many segmented, multilobed cells around the infected ones fill the field because gonococci provoke a purulent exudate, so a Gram stain of discharge shows abundant polymorphonuclear cells besides the bacteria.
